skills.trigger: When evaluating serial chest radiographs to determine the etiology of co-occurring findings (e.g., pleural effusion and parenchymal opacity) based on their differential resolution rates.
steps: Compare the baseline and follow-up images to assess the change in volume/density of the pleural effusion versus the adjacent lung opacity.
Identify if the effusion has resolved or significantly decreased while the parenchymal opacity persists or becomes more distinct.

Conclude that rapid resolution of fluid with persistent opacity suggests the fluid was an acute/transient reaction (e.g., parapneumonic) masking a chronic underlying lung pathology, rather than a single acute process resolving uniformly.

skills.trigger: When assessing the retrocardiac region on frontal chest radiographs, especially when a pleural effusion is present or resolving.
steps: Inspect the retrocardiac density behind the heart shadow, looking for increased opacity that obscures the left hemidiaphragm or descending aorta.
Distinguish this finding from the silhouette of the heart itself by checking for loss of normal borders (silhouette sign).
Note that this opacity may be partially hidden by superimposed pleural fluid initially and only become clearly definable as a distinct parenchymal abnormality once the fluid clears.
